stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Okafor's conclusion?
stimulus:
Most printed maps put north at the top. Many digital navigation apps instead rotate the map so that the direction the traveler is facing is always up. Cartographer Lena Okafor and her colleagues asked volunteers to walk unfamiliar routes with one of the two map styles and counted their wrong turns. The volunteers were grouped by whether they had any prior orienteering experience. Okafor concluded that turning the map to match the traveler's heading reduces navigation errors among novice map readers.

Average Wrong Turns per Route
Map reader | North-up map | Heading-up map
Novice | 4.2 | 1.8
Experienced | 1.1 | 1.0
choices: Experienced readers averaged 1.1 wrong turns with north-up maps and 1.0 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
Novice readers averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps and 1.8 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
Novice readers averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps, while experienced readers averaged 1.1 wrong turns.
Novice readers averaged 1.8 wrong turns with north-up maps and 4.2 wrong turns with heading-up maps.
explanation: Okafor's conclusion is about one group, novice readers, and one comparison: heading-up maps versus north-up maps. To support it, you need novice readers to make fewer wrong turns with heading-up maps. Choice B shows exactly that: 1.8 wrong turns compared with 4.2.

A.why: These numbers are accurate, but they describe experienced readers. The conclusion is limited to novices, so you compared the right map styles for the wrong group.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares novices with experienced readers who were both using north-up maps. The conclusion is about the effect of map style, and this choice never compares the two styles.

D.why: You swapped the columns. In the table, novices averaged 4.2 wrong turns with north-up maps, not with heading-up maps. Read this way, the data would weaken the conclusion.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the planners' hypothesis?
stimulus:
A city transportation office studied 12 pairs of streets. The two streets in each pair had similar traffic, width and nearby housing. One street in each pair had a bike lane marked only with paint. The other had a lane separated from cars by a raised curb. The office counted cyclists on both streets for six months. Because commuters tend to avoid riding next to heavy rush-hour traffic, the planners hypothesized that curb-separated lanes draw more cyclists than painted lanes on weekdays.

Average Daily Cyclists per Street
Lane type | Weekdays | Weekends
Painted lane | 310 | 420
Curb-separated lane | 680 | 450
choices: On weekends, streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 450 cyclists, and streets with painted lanes averaged 420.
Streets with painted lanes averaged 420 cyclists on weekends but only 310 cyclists on weekdays.
On weekdays, streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 680 cyclists, and streets with painted lanes averaged 310.
On weekdays, streets with painted lanes averaged 680 cyclists, and streets with curb-separated lanes averaged 310.
explanation: The hypothesis applies only to weekdays and compares the two lane types. To support it, the curb-separated lanes need more weekday cyclists than the painted lanes. Choice C reports that comparison: 680 cyclists versus 310.

A.why: The numbers are right, but they come from the weekend column. The hypothesis is limited to weekdays, so this choice skips the condition the claim depends on.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares days of the week for one lane type. The hypothesis needs a comparison between the two lane types, and this choice never makes one.

D.why: You attached the weekday numbers to the wrong lane types. The table gives 680 for curb-separated lanes and 310 for painted lanes. Read this way, the data would weaken the hypothesis.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Reyes's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Fresh snow reflects most incoming sunlight and gives off heat efficiently into a clear night sky, so the ground under it cools quickly after sunset. The chilled surface then cools the layer of air just above it. Meteorologist Tomás Reyes compared overnight low temperatures at weather stations on a valley floor and on a nearby ridge. He sorted nights with snow on the ground from nights without it. Reyes hypothesizes that snow cover produces much colder nights at valley-floor stations.

Average Overnight Low (°C)
Station location | Snow-covered nights | Bare-ground nights
Valley floor | −14 | −7
Ridge top | −9 | −8
choices: At valley-floor stations, the average low was −14°C on snow-covered nights and −7°C on bare-ground nights.
At ridge-top stations, the average low was −9°C on snow-covered nights and −8°C on bare-ground nights.
On snow-covered nights, the average low was −14°C at valley-floor stations and −9°C at ridge-top stations.
At valley-floor stations, the average low was −7°C on snow-covered nights and −14°C on bare-ground nights.
explanation: The hypothesis is about valley-floor stations, and it compares nights with snow to nights without it. Choice A stays on the valley floor and shows that snow-covered nights were much colder: −14°C compared with −7°C.

B.why: The numbers are accurate, but they come from the ridge-top row. The hypothesis is limited to valley-floor stations, so this is the right comparison in the wrong place.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares the two locations on snowy nights. The hypothesis is about whether snow makes valley nights colder, so you need snow and bare ground at the same location.

D.why: You reversed the valley-floor values. In the table, the −14°C low goes with snow-covered nights, not bare-ground nights.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Nandakumar's conclusion?
stimulus:
Madder root produces a red dye that does not bond well to fibers by itself. Dyers in medieval Europe often soaked cloth in alum first. Alum is a mineral salt that binds to both the fiber and the dye. Textile historian Priya Nandakumar re-created this process. She dyed samples of wool and linen with madder, some with alum and some without, and then washed each sample twenty times. She concludes that alum was essential to the long-lasting reds of medieval woolens.

Color Retained After 20 Washes (%)
Fiber | With alum | Without alum
Wool | 85 | 40
Linen | 45 | 30
choices: Linen samples dyed with alum retained 45% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 30%.
Wool and linen samples dyed with alum retained 85% and 45% of their color, respectively.
Wool samples dyed with alum retained 40% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 85%.
Wool samples dyed with alum retained 85% of their color, and those dyed without alum retained 40%.
explanation: The conclusion is about woolens, and it says alum made the difference. To support it, you need wool dyed with alum compared with wool dyed without alum. Choice D shows wool keeping 85% of its color with alum and only 40% without it.

A.why: These figures are accurate, but they describe linen. The conclusion is about woolens, so you made the right comparison for the wrong fabric.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares two fabrics that were both treated with alum. To show that alum was essential, you have to compare samples with alum to samples without it.

C.why: You swapped the wool columns. In the table, the wool dyed with alum is the sample that retained 85% of its color.

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Sato's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Spiral galaxies have lanes of dust concentrated in their flat disks. When we see a galaxy edge-on, starlight has to pass through much more of that dust than when we see the galaxy face-on. Dust absorbs visible light far more strongly than infrared light. For that reason, astronomer Hana Sato expected a galaxy's orientation to matter mainly for one kind of measurement. She hypothesizes that edge-on spirals appear substantially dimmer than face-on spirals in visible light.

Average Surface Brightness of Spiral Galaxies (relative units)
Orientation | Visible light | Infrared light
Face-on | 80 | 60
Edge-on | 35 | 58
choices: In infrared light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 58 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 60.
Face-on spirals had an average brightness of 80 units in visible light and 60 units in infrared light.
In visible light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 35 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 80.
In visible light, edge-on spirals had an average brightness of 80 units, and face-on spirals had an average of 35.
explanation: The hypothesis is limited to visible light, and it says edge-on spirals should look dimmer than face-on spirals. Choice C uses the visible-light column and shows that edge-on galaxies were much dimmer: 35 units compared with 80.

A.why: These values are accurate, but they come from the infrared column. The hypothesis covers visible light only, so this choice skips the condition the claim depends on.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares two kinds of light for face-on galaxies only. The hypothesis is about how edge-on and face-on galaxies differ, and this choice never compares them.

D.why: You assigned the visible-light values to the wrong orientations. The table gives 35 units for edge-on spirals and 80 for face-on spirals.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?
stimulus:
Many respiratory viruses spread most easily in the colder months, when students spend more time indoors. A team of public health researchers put hand-sanitizer stations in every classroom at six elementary schools. They then compared illness-related absences at those schools with absences at six similar schools that had no stations. The researchers concluded that the stations reduced illness-related absences, but only during winter.

Average Illness-Related Absences (per 100 students per month)
School group | Fall | Winter
With stations | 3 | 4
Without stations | 3 | 9
choices: In winter, schools with stations averaged 4 illness-related absences per 100 students, compared with 9 at schools without stations.
In fall, schools with stations and schools without stations each averaged 3 illness-related absences per 100 students.
Schools without stations averaged 9 illness-related absences per 100 students in winter, up from 3 in fall.
In winter, schools with stations averaged 9 illness-related absences per 100 students, compared with 4 at schools without stations.
explanation: The conclusion says the stations reduced absences during winter. To support that, you need to compare the two school groups in the Winter column. Schools with stations had 4 absences per 100 students and schools without had 9, so absences were lower where there were stations.

B.why: This is accurate, but it describes fall, when the two groups don't differ. The conclusion is about winter. This choice shows no reduction, so it can't support the claim that the stations reduced absences.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares one group across two seasons instead of comparing schools with and without stations. A rise in winter at schools without stations doesn't show that the stations made any difference.

D.why: This swaps the two winter values. The table shows 4 absences at schools with stations and 9 at schools without. As written, this choice would mean the stations went with more absences.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the astronomer's hypothesis?
stimulus:
Stellar flares are sudden bursts of radiation that can strip the atmospheres from nearby planets. Red dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy, so their flares affect estimates of how many planets could be habitable. Using telescope data, astronomer Tomas Reyes counted flares on red dwarfs and on Sun-like stars of different ages. Reyes hypothesizes that young red dwarfs flare more often than old red dwarfs do.

Average Flares Observed per Day
Star type | Young (under 1 billion years) | Old (over 5 billion years)
Red dwarf | 12 | 2
Sun-like | 3 | 1
choices: Young red dwarfs averaged 12 flares per day, whereas young Sun-like stars averaged 3 flares per day.
Young red dwarfs averaged 12 flares per day, whereas old red dwarfs averaged 2 flares per day.
Young Sun-like stars averaged 3 flares per day, whereas old Sun-like stars averaged 1 flare per day.
Young red dwarfs averaged 2 flares per day, whereas old red dwarfs averaged 12 flares per day.
explanation: The hypothesis compares red dwarfs of two ages. That means you stay in the Red dwarf row and compare Young with Old. Young red dwarfs averaged 12 flares per day and old ones averaged 2, which is the difference the hypothesis predicts.

A.why: Both numbers are correct, but this compares two star types of the same age. The hypothesis compares young and old red dwarfs, so this choice uses the wrong series.

C.why: This shows the right pattern for the wrong kind of star. Sun-like stars losing flare activity with age tells you nothing about red dwarfs, so you would be applying one group's result to another.

D.why: This swaps the Red dwarf values. The table shows 12 flares for young red dwarfs and 2 for old ones, not the other way around. As written, this choice would weaken the hypothesis.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Lindqvist's claim?
stimulus:
Many folk songs open with a short phrase that comes back several times. Musicologist Hana Lindqvist wondered whether this feature makes a tune easier to learn by ear. She played unfamiliar folk melodies, some with a repeated opening phrase and some without, to listeners with and without formal musical training. She tested their recall a day later. Lindqvist claims that a repeated opening helps listeners without training recall a melody.

Melodies Recalled Correctly After One Day (%)
Listener group | Repeated opening | No repeated opening
Trained | 80 | 76
Untrained | 70 | 40
choices: Untrained listeners recalled 70 percent of melodies with a repeated opening and 40 percent of melodies without one.
Trained listeners recalled 80 percent of melodies with a repeated opening and 76 percent of melodies without one.
For melodies with a repeated opening, trained listeners recalled 80 percent and untrained listeners recalled 70 percent.
Untrained listeners recalled 40 percent of melodies with a repeated opening and 70 percent of melodies without one.
explanation: The claim is about listeners without training, so stay in the Untrained row. Then compare melodies with a repeated opening to melodies without one. Untrained listeners recalled 70 percent with the repeated opening and 40 percent without it, so the repeated opening helped them.

B.why: These numbers are accurate, but they belong to trained listeners. The claim is limited to listeners without training, so this choice compares the right conditions in the wrong group.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares two listener groups under one condition. To show that a repeated opening helps, you have to compare melodies with and without one.

D.why: This swaps the Untrained values. The table shows 70 percent recalled with a repeated opening and 40 percent without it. As written, this choice would suggest the repeated opening made recall worse.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the engineers' hypothesis?
stimulus:
Porous asphalt has open gaps that let rainwater drain through the pavement into a gravel layer below. To test the material, civil engineers paved two neighboring sections of the same road. The sections were identical except that one used standard asphalt and the other used porous asphalt. The engineers hypothesized that the porous section would hold less standing water than the standard section after heavy rainfall.

Standing Water One Hour After Rainfall (millimeters)
Rainfall | Standard asphalt | Porous asphalt
Light | 2 | 0
Heavy | 14 | 3
choices: After light rainfall, the standard section held 2 millimeters of standing water and the porous section held 0.
After heavy rainfall, the porous section held 3 millimeters of standing water, compared with 0 after light rainfall.
After heavy rainfall, the standard section held 3 millimeters of standing water and the porous section held 14.
After heavy rainfall, the standard section held 14 millimeters of standing water and the porous section held 3.
explanation: The hypothesis applies only after heavy rainfall, so use the Heavy row. Then compare the two pavement types. The standard section held 14 millimeters and the porous section held 3, so the porous section held less standing water.

A.why: This compares the right pavements under the wrong condition. The hypothesis is specifically about heavy rainfall, and this choice reports only light rainfall.

B.why: This is accurate, but it compares the porous section with itself under two rainfall levels. The hypothesis requires comparing porous asphalt with standard asphalt.

C.why: This swaps the two Heavy values. The table shows 14 millimeters on the standard section and 3 on the porous section. As written, this choice would weaken the hypothesis.

stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the planners' conclusion?
stimulus:
Many cyclists avoid busy streets because they feel unsafe sharing lanes with cars. If a physical barrier makes riders feel safer, more people may choose to cycle. A city installed protected bike lanes on several commercial streets and several residential streets, and it counted bicycle trips before and after the installation. City planners concluded that the protected lanes increased cycling on commercial streets.

Average Daily Bicycle Trips per Street
Street type | Before lanes | After lanes
Commercial | 300 | 600
Residential | 200 | 220
choices: On residential streets, average daily bicycle trips rose from 200 before the lanes to 220 after the lanes.
On commercial streets, average daily bicycle trips rose from 300 before the lanes to 600 after the lanes.
After the lanes opened, commercial streets averaged 600 daily bicycle trips and residential streets averaged 220.
On commercial streets, average daily bicycle trips fell from 600 before the lanes to 300 after the lanes.
explanation: The conclusion is limited to commercial streets and says cycling increased. Use the Commercial row and compare Before with After. Trips rose from 300 to 600, which is the increase the planners describe.

A.why: This is accurate, but it reports residential streets. The conclusion is about commercial streets, so this choice uses the wrong series.

C.why: This is accurate, but it compares two street types after the lanes opened. It doesn't show any change over time, so it can't show that the lanes increased cycling.

D.why: This swaps the Before and After values for commercial streets. The table shows trips rising from 300 to 600. As written, this choice would mean the lanes reduced cycling.
